claims.text: The demand for a factor of production is the quantity of a factor - land, labour, capital or enterprise - that firms are willing and able to employ at a given cost over a period of time.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The demand for factors of production is a derived demand: firms employ workers and machines because of consumers' demand for the goods and services those factors produce, so a change in the market for a finished good tends to move the demand for the factors that make it in the same direction.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A firm's demand for a factor tends to rise with demand for its product, and tends to be checked by the factor's cost: a higher wage makes a firm cautious about hiring and may lead it to use equipment instead, while greater productivity can let fewer workers cover the same orders.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The demand for goods and the demand for factors of production are different demands: consumers demand goods and services for the satisfaction they give, while firms demand factors in order to produce output for others to buy; the test is to ask who is buying and for what purpose.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Labour-intensive production is production in which workers carry out most of the work, so wages form the greater share of the firm's costs; capital-intensive production is production in which machinery and equipment carry out most of the work, so capital costs form the greater share.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The boundary between labour-intensive and capital-intensive production is the share of the work, or of cost, carried by labour against capital; most firms use both factors, and intensity is a matter of degree rather than a pair of boxes.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A firm's choice between labour-intensive and capital-intensive methods tends to depend on the relative cost of workers and machines, the size of its market, the funds it can raise, and whether its product needs craft variety or uniformity; neither method suits every firm.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Production is the total quantity of goods or services a firm makes in a period, measured in units such as bottles or chairs.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Productivity is output per unit of a factor of production over a period; labour productivity is total output divided by the number of workers, measured for example in bottles per worker.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Where productivity rises, the wage bill is spread over more units, so cost per unit tends to fall and the firm can cut its price or earn more per unit sold; where productivity falls, cost per unit tends to rise.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Production is a total and productivity is a rate per factor of production; two firms with equal production can differ in productivity, and production can rise while productivity falls where extra workers add less output per worker than the existing workers did.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The availability of a factor influences a firm's demand for it: where a factor is scarce in an area - skilled workers, suitable land, or machines that must be imported - a firm may be unable to employ as much of it as it wants and may turn to factors that are easier to obtain, while a factor in plentiful supply tends to be cheaper and quicker to employ.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A more productive factor produces more output for each N$ spent on it, so firms tend to prefer it to less productive alternatives, while the number of units of it they employ also depends on whether demand for the product is growing.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Production in a period depends on the quantity of factors of production a firm employs, on their productivity, and on the demand for the product, since firms tend to produce what they expect to sell; production can rise through adding more factors even where productivity is unchanged.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Productivity tends to rise with education and training, more and better capital and technology, workers' motivation, better management and organisation of work, and better-quality inputs; a rise in productivity means each unit of a factor produces more, not simply that more factors are employed.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.
